documents.title: Faculty Resources for Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Generative AI
documents.summary: A Learning and Educational Center page of guidance for faculty on generative AI. It sets no student rule; it advises on syllabus statements, talking with students, disclosure, privacy, detector limits and redesigning courses, and points to NSU's separate AI policy site.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no stance for students. It says 'Effectively integrating Generative AI requires both proactive conversations with students and a clear syllabus policy' and 'Be clear with students ... as to when it is appropriate to use these tools for your courses', leaving each instructor to decide.

units.why: Names a licensed tool all faculty and staff can use: 'have access to Microsoft Copilot, your AI assistant for education'. That is a sanctioned institutional tool (P17); it is an access statement rather than a rule, so modality informs.
units.anchor: All faculty and staff have access to Microsoft Copilot

units.why: The page frames GenAI as a 'Faculty Assistant' that can 'refine existing materials' and free time, which encourages instructor use of AI for teaching work (P59, not P47/P48 because it does not speak of disclosure or review).
units.anchor: Empower your teaching and scholarship with Generative AI

units.why: States 'AI detection tools often result in false positives and false negatives', so detectors are unreliable (P39); it is a factual claim, hence informs.
units.anchor: AI detection tools often result in false positives and false negatives

units.why: Adds that false positives are more frequent for second-language writers, weak writers and autistic students. Same point as the detector-unreliability type (P39), with an equity angle the type does not name.
units.anchor: higher frequency of false positives among students writing in a second language
units.fit_note: Adds that detector errors fall unevenly on second-language writers, students with poor writing skills and autistic students.

units.why: Says three higher-education bodies 'caution faculty against putting their faith in AI detection tools'; this is advice not to rely on detectors (P39), phrased as caution so should-not.
units.anchor: caution faculty against putting their faith in AI detection tools

units.why: Recommends faculty 'restructure their courses to reduce the temptation to use AI tools', i.e. redesign assignments around AI (P35).
units.anchor: recommend that faculty restructure their courses to reduce the temptation to use AI tools

units.why: Gives concrete redesign options: 'incorporating more in-class activities, breaking up large assignments into multi-stage projects, or requiring students to articulate their workflow'. All are assignment redesign (P35), though in-class activity and workflow articulation also touch P33/P34; P35 is the broadest fit.
units.anchor: breaking up large assignments into multi-stage projects, or requiring students to articulate their workflow

units.why: Says faculty 'may need to provide opportunities to practice higher-order thinking skills on low stakes assignments'; a course-design recommendation (P35).
units.anchor: provide opportunities to practice higher-order thinking skills on low stakes assignments

units.why: Explains that students put the 'short-term goal of producing work that gets a high grade' above 'developing their own thinking and writing skills'. It is a rationale about skill-building being displaced (nearest P41); P41 is about limiting AI because practice builds skill, this describes the motive for misuse.
units.anchor: The short-term goal of producing work that gets a high grade is often more important
units.fit_note: Describes why students outsource work (grade over skill) rather than stating a limit on AI use.

units.why: Says 'Faculty can use Generative AI for a variety of administrative tasks', giving permission for instructor use of AI (P59).
units.anchor: Faculty can use Generative AI for a variety of administrative tasks

units.why: Says 'Outputs from generative AI should always be reviewed for accuracy, accessibility, and inclusivity'. It is about checking AI output (P31) though aimed at faculty and covering accessibility and inclusivity as well as accuracy.
units.anchor: Outputs from generative AI should always be reviewed for accuracy, accessibility, and inclusivity
units.fit_note: Review covers accessibility and inclusivity as well as accuracy, and is addressed to faculty.

units.why: Says personal emails 'may need to be edited so the voice of the writer is apparent'. A rule on how instructors use AI drafts in communication (P59).
units.anchor: emails and other personal communication may need to be edited so the voice

units.why: Says 'names, ID numbers, and any other information that identifies people should not be included in any generative AI prompt or chat': personal-data protection (P50).
units.anchor: should not be included in any generative AI prompt or chat

units.why: 'Compliance with University policies is always a requirement' ties AI use to existing university policy (P77).
units.anchor: Compliance with University policies is always a requirement

units.why: Tells faculty to 'make sure that the generative AI tools you are using comply with University policy and appropriate security classifications'. Compliance duty (P77) rather than a vetted-tool preference (P50), since it names policy and security classifications.
units.anchor: tools you are using comply with University policy and appropriate security classifications

units.why: Says AI 'is not a replacement for the researcher, but rather a tool' for research, and lists uses such as summaries and literature reviews. This governs AI in research and scholarship (P62), permissively.
units.anchor: It is not a replacement for the researcher, but rather a tool

units.why: Names research uses that are 'most beneficial': 'summarize or paraphrase content', discover gaps, support a literature review. Permissive guidance on AI in research (P62).
units.anchor: Some of the most beneficial uses of AI tools in research involve the ability to

units.why: Warns that 'you should always take a critical view of any AI results and not become to overly dependent on them': verify AI output (P31).
units.anchor: you should always take a critical view of any AI results
units.frag_start: It is useful to remember that

units.why: Says tools 'can also mislead you into thinking that you don't need to do your own reading, summary and analysis'. The risk is substituting AI for your own thinking, so P32.
units.anchor: mislead you into thinking that you don't need to do your own reading
units.frag_start: They can also mislead you into
units.fit_note: About AI research tools in faculty research, not student work.

units.why: Says 'Effectively integrating Generative AI requires both proactive conversations with students and a clear syllabus policy'. It asks for a syllabus policy (P09) and conversations; P09 chosen because 'clear syllabus policy' is the explicit requirement, P66 is covered in the following units.
units.anchor: requires both proactive conversations with students and a clear syllabus policy
units.fit_note: Pairs a syllabus policy with proactive student conversations; a recommendation, not a mandate.

units.why: 'Explain the reasoning behind your policy and its implications' asks instructors to give students the reasons for their AI rules (P66).
units.anchor: Explain the reasoning behind your policy and its implications

units.why: 'Discuss your policy in multiple places, at multiple times, and in multiple ways' recommends repeated discussion beyond listing the rule (P66).
units.anchor: Discuss your policy in multiple places, at multiple times, and in multiple ways

units.why: Advises placing the policy 'near the front of the syllabus or somewhere near your sections on plagiarism and citation'. Where to state the AI policy in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: place your policy near the front of the syllabus
units.fit_note: Concerns placement and prominence of the syllabus statement rather than requiring one.

units.why: 'include a discussion of Generative AI tools in the descriptions or instructions for individual assignments' asks for AI expectations in assignment instructions (P09, which covers assignment instructions).
units.anchor: include a discussion of Generative AI tools in the descriptions or instructions for individual assignments

units.why: 'Discuss with your students verbally at the beginning of a course and also during relevant portions of the course' recommends in-class discussion of AI rules (P66).
units.anchor: Discuss with your students verbally at the beginning of a course

units.why: 'Provide resources about AI, its uses, ethical debates, plagiarism, citation' gives students AI-literacy material (P70).
units.anchor: Provide resources about AI, its uses, ethical debates, plagiarism, citation
units.fit_note: Instructor-provided reading list rather than an institutional training or module.

units.why: 'Use plain, direct, and accurate language during generative AI discussions' is advice on wording the rules (P66).
units.anchor: Use plain, direct, and accurate language during generative AI discussions

units.why: Tells instructors to 'Explain the value of what you're teaching to your students and the value of them learning it for themselves', giving reasons for limits. Closest is P66 (explain the rules), although the content echoes P41.
units.anchor: Explain the value of what you're teaching to your students
units.fit_note: Also stresses the learning-value rationale (P41) and treats AI ethics as a conversation starter.

units.why: 'Make students aware of the potential pitfalls of Generative AI, such as bias and hallucinations' asks instructors to teach about bias and error. P53 names bias; hallucination is P31, but bias is named first.
units.anchor: Make students aware of the potential pitfalls of Generative AI, such as bias and hallucinations

units.why: 'Don't be afraid to discuss the gray areas with your students' invites open discussion of unclear AI uses (P66).
units.anchor: Don't be afraid to discuss the gray areas with your students

units.why: 'Encourage your students to use proper citations. Communicate your preferred method of citation to them.' This is a recommendation that students cite AI use (P24).
units.anchor: Encourage your students to use proper citations

units.why: Asks instructors to have students 'be honest and open to share their prompts, share their results wherever relevant, and how they use them'. Naming prompts and results fits P25.
units.anchor: Ask them to be honest and open to share their prompts, share their results

units.why: 'give them some insight into how Generative AI will be used in their future careers and disciplines' teaches AI as a professional matter (P44).
units.anchor: give them some insight into how Generative AI will be used in their future careers

units.why: 'the tools are a good starting point, but they need outside sources, knowledge, and information to assess the results' means verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: they need outside sources, knowledge, and information to assess the results

units.why: 'Guide your students in using generative AI tools, such as writing queries, analyzing results, interrogating the bots' responses' means teaching effective AI use (P44).
units.anchor: Guide your students in using generative AI tools, such as writing queries

units.why: 'Encourage your students to come to you if they have questions about how to use these tools' invites students to ask before acting (P10), seen from the instructor's side.
units.anchor: Encourage your students to come to you if they have questions
units.fit_note: Framed as an instructor duty to invite questions, not a student duty to ask first.

units.why: Says access to GenAI is uneven because of 'the digital divide, lack of technical knowledge and economic barriers' and 'is important to keep in mind as the expectations for students to access and use Generative AI are developed'. Equity concern (P51).
units.anchor: important to keep in mind as the expectations for students to access and use Generative
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to weigh unequal access when setting expectations; does not say AI must be optional.

units.why: States that GenAI 'has the potential to significantly improve accessibility for people with disabilities'. Not a rule about permitted uses or equity of access, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: potential to significantly improve accessibility for people with disabilities
units.uncovered_note: AI as an accessibility aid for people with disabilities (captions, descriptions, adaptive support), plus accessibility risks of AI output.

units.why: Notes AI 'can generate inaccessible content' and that 'users of AI can be intentional with data input to ensure the output is accessible'. A caution about accessibility of AI output; no type covers it.
units.anchor: users of AI can be intentional with data input to ensure the output is accessible
units.uncovered_note: Users should check that AI output is accessible (alt-text, speech recognition limits).

units.why: 'maintaining awareness of such outcomes can help us use GenAI responsibly' asks for awareness of AI's energy and resource costs (P53).
units.anchor: maintaining awareness of such outcomes can help us use GenAI responsibly

units.why: Lists ethical problems: 'academic or professional dishonesty' and bias from training data (P53).
units.anchor: Bias is also a major concern, since these models are trained on a wide range

units.why: Raises 'concerns about intellectual property, since these models are often trained on content that wasn't approved for use by the authors': copyright of AI inputs and outputs (P52).
units.anchor: concerns about intellectual property, since these models are often trained on content

units.why: 'it is also valuable to educate students about them so that they can be aware and develop their genAI literacy skills' recommends teaching students about AI ethics (P70).
units.anchor: educate students about them so that they can be aware and develop their genAI literacy
units.fit_note: Instructor-led, course-level education rather than an institutional program.

units.why: 'Let students know that while there are appropriate uses for genAI, there are also inappropriate and unethical uses' tells instructors to explain where lines fall (P66).
units.anchor: there are also inappropriate and unethical uses

units.why: 'Be clear with students, both verbally and in written policies, as to when it is appropriate to use these tools for your courses and whether and how they should disclose' asks for a stated course-level AI rule including disclosure (P09).
units.anchor: Be clear with students, both verbally and in written policies, as to when it is
units.fit_note: Also says the statement should cover whether and how students disclose AI use.

units.why: Says 'Giving students guided exposure to genAI in their coursework builds the GenAI literacy skills' employers want; AI is taught as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: Giving students guided exposure to genAI in their coursework builds the GenAI literacy skills

units.why: 'It is useful to consider this when designing courses and making curricular decisions that will affect students' career readiness' links curriculum to AI career readiness (P44).
units.anchor: when designing courses and making curricular decisions that will affect students' career readiness
units.frag_start: It is useful to consider this

units.why: Says tools 'can also often return information that is inaccurate or completely made up', i.e. hallucinations (P31).
units.anchor: they can also often return information that is inaccurate or completely made up

units.why: 'it is also valuable to educate students on GenAI hallucinations so they know they need to scrutinize results for accuracy' asks instructors to teach students to verify output (P31).
units.anchor: educate students on GenAI hallucinations so they know they need to scrutinize results for accuracy
units.frag_start: It is also valuable to educate

units.why: 'Generative AI tools use information from prompts and results to further train the models' explains why prompts are not private (P50).
units.anchor: Generative AI tools use information from prompts and results to further train the models
units.frag_end: found by others in the future.

units.why: 'It is advised that you refrain from putting any personal data or proprietary information into these tools': protect personal and proprietary data (P50).
units.anchor: refrain from putting any personal data or proprietary information into these tools
units.frag_start: It is advised that you refrain

units.why: 'All FERPA guidelines should be considered when it comes to data privacy and genAI' ties AI use to existing law (P77).
units.anchor: All FERPA guidelines should be considered when it comes to data privacy and genAI

units.why: 'Identifiable information, like names and personal data, should be removed from any inputs' is a data-minimization step (P50).
units.anchor: Identifiable information, like names and personal data, should be removed from any inputs

units.why: 'Proprietary content should not be put into genAI tools' bars putting protected content into AI. It is a bar on uploading protected materials (P49) addressed to faculty, with the exception for NSU-approved tools in the next unit.
units.anchor: Proprietary content should not be put into genAI tools
units.fit_note: Addressed to faculty and staff, covering proprietary content generally, not only course materials uploaded by students.

units.why: Says for 'NSU-approved tools' faculty 'may consider allowing course content or other NSU content'. It sets an approved-tools exception to the data rule (P17).
units.anchor: you may consider allowing course content or other NSU content
units.fit_note: Concerns permission to enter course content into NSU-approved tools, not provision of a tool.

units.why: 'information such as financial data, social security numbers, etc. should never be put into any tool whether NSU-approved or not' is an absolute data ban (P50).
units.anchor: should never be put into any tool whether NSU-approved or not

units.why: 'Please check NSU guidance and policy regularly to keep track of which genAI tools have been officially approved' points to vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: keep track of which genAI tools have been officially approved for use

units.why: 'Use the F.A.S.T.E.R principle to help ensure Generative AI is being used responsibly' offers a principles framework for responsible use (P56).
units.anchor: to help ensure Generative AI is being used responsibly

units.why: Suggests responsible-use scenarios 'can be used with students as an activity or to generate discussions on the appropriate use of GenAI' (P66, discuss AI use in class).
units.anchor: can be used with students as an activity or to generate discussions on the appropriate

units.why: Points faculty to the Mako Commons virtual community of practice to 'connect with NSU faculty to share ideas, information, and resources': faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: connect with NSU faculty to share ideas, information, and resources

units.why: The page says it exists 'to familiarize, support, and guide Nova Southeastern University faculty in AI matters', which sets its purpose and scope (P63, faculty support).
units.anchor: serves to familiarize, support, and guide Nova Southeastern University faculty in AI matters

units.why: 'We Welcome Your Feedback! If you would like to propose content to be added to this page' invites feedback and indicates the page is revised (P54).
units.anchor: If you would like to propose content to be added to this page

documents.unit: Office of the Provost / Student Handbook (academic standards)
documents.title: Student Handbook 2025-2026: Academic Standards (generative AI clause)
documents.summary: The 2025-26 Student Handbook's academic-standards section, within its original-work standard, prohibits generative AI on coursework or assessments without prior faculty permission, or in ways that violate academic standards. It is a single sentence on AI.
documents.stance_why: The handbook says AI use on any coursework 'without the prior permission of their faculty member ... is expressly prohibited'. Ban by default, permitted when the faculty member allows, so restrict.

units.why: The handbook says student 'use of generative artificial intelligence ... on any coursework or academic assessments without the prior permission of their faculty member ... is expressly prohibited'. AI is banned unless the instructor permits it, which is the fallback-with-permission rule (P06) rather than P01 because permission by faculty lifts the ban.
units.anchor: without the prior permission of their faculty member
units.fit_note: Ban is on all coursework and assessments, with permission resting with the individual faculty member.

units.why: Same sentence also bars use 'in any way that violates the academic standards of NSU and/or a student's academic program'. This ties AI use to the existing academic standards and treats violation as breach of them (P36), separate from the permission rule.
units.anchor: violates the academic standards of NSU and/or a student's academic program
units.fit_note: Classifies as violation of academic standards via prohibition; no penalty or process is named.

notes: Coder B. Doc 1 points to NSU's separate AI website for the university AI policy; that page was not in the collected text, so it is not coded. Handbook: only the single generative AI sentence was coded. Many instructor-facing advice units use unit_stance neutral because they recommend practices rather than take a position on student AI use.
